_comment: Roster for the 'is this you?' claim pages under /agi/yours/<slug>/.
Regenerate the pages with: node scripts/build-claim-pages.mjs
corpusCount is the number of INDEXED sources the room's AI host actually retrieves
over — read from each site's netlify/edge-lib/corpus-index.js (docs.length), not from
papers.json. If the corpora are rebuilt, re-read those numbers before regenerating;
a wrong count on a page addressed to the author of the corpus is the worst possible
hook is one hand-written line per person: the difference between a note and a form
letter. Every hook makes the same argument in that person's own material — the room
has the published work and is missing the person. Keep them specific, defensible from
public record, and free of second-guessing about what anyone privately thinks.

speakers.name: Karl Friston
speakers.hostConcept: the Markov blanket — the statistical boundary that makes a thing a thing
speakers.hook: Right now the room can tell you what a Markov blanket is, straight out of your papers. It can't tell you why you kept reaching for that idea for thirty years. That part isn't in the corpus, because it was never published — it's in you.

speakers.name: Christof Koch
speakers.hostConcept: Φ — the integrated information measure at the centre of IIT
speakers.hook: The room can define Φ. It cannot answer the person who walks up and says IIT is unfalsifiable — not the way you'd answer them, with whatever you actually concede and whatever you don't.

speakers.name: Alison Gopnik
speakers.hostConcept: lantern consciousness — the wide, diffuse attention of young children
speakers.hook: The room knows lantern consciousness as it appears in the papers. It doesn't have the version you'd use on someone who has never read a paper and is holding a four-year-old — and that's the version that actually travels.

speakers.name: Anil Seth
speakers.hostConcept: the felt, embodied glow — the beast machine, interoception, consciousness from the inside out
speakers.hook: The room can recite controlled hallucination accurately. What it can't do is the move you make in public where you stop and name the experiment that would show you were wrong.

speakers.name: Ben Goertzel
speakers.hostConcept: the AtomSpace — the knowledge representation at the heart of OpenCog
speakers.hook: The room knows AtomSpace and Hyperon as documented. It doesn't carry the decades of why-this-and-not-that behind the architecture, which is most of what anyone building on it actually needs.

speakers.name: Gary Marcus
speakers.hostConcept: innate scaffolding — the prior structure that learning needs
speakers.hook: The room can make your argument. It cannot make it the way you make it, and — whatever anyone thinks of the argument — the way you make it is a distinctive instrument that a stock voice flattens into nothing.

speakers.name: David Eagleman
speakers.hostConcept: umwelt — the slice of reality an organism can perceive
speakers.hook: The room knows umwelt from the writing. It doesn't have your instinct for the one demonstration that makes a stranger understand it in ten seconds, and that instinct is not recoverable from a corpus.

speakers.name: Chris Fields
speakers.hostConcept: the holographic screen — the informational boundary of any observer
speakers.hook: The room can quote the holographic-screen formalism cleanly. It can't tell anyone which parts you consider settled and which parts you're still arguing with yourself about — and for work this far out on the frontier, that distinction is the useful information.

speakers.name: David Spivak
speakers.hostConcept: the olog — an ontology log, category theory made writable
speakers.hook: The room can define an olog. It can't sit across from someone with a messy domain and walk them into building one, which is the part of applied category theory that actually changes how a person thinks.

speakers.name: Alexander Ororbia
speakers.hostConcept: the synapse — the local, biologically plausible learning rule
speakers.hook: The room knows predictive coding as published. It doesn't know what you think backpropagation got right — a better question than what it got wrong, and one nobody can answer from the papers alone.

speakers.name: Michael Levin
speakers.hostConcept: target morphology — the anatomical goal state a collective of cells navigates toward
speakers.corpusKind: published papers, recorded talks, essays and a dictionary of terms
speakers.hook: The room holds five hundred indexed sources and answers about target morphology well. What it doesn't have is the move you make where a question about frogs becomes a question about minds — the corpus records that you did it, not how.

speakers.name: Joscha Bach
speakers.hostConcept: cyber-animism — minds as software running on any sufficient substrate
speakers.corpusKind: public threads and a dictionary of terms
speakers.hook: The room carries three hundred and fifty-eight of your public threads. It has your conclusions. It does not have your timing — and with you, the timing is half the argument.
